questions.prompt: Which wall was built across northern Britain by order of an emperor in AD 122?
questions.fact: A later emperor built a second wall further north, held it for about twenty years, then abandoned it and fell back to this one.

questions.prompt: The Rosetta Stone is written in three scripts. Which is not one of them?
questions.fact: Greek was the key: scholars could already read it, which let them work backwards into the two Egyptian scripts.

questions.prompt: Which city was the capital of the Aztec Empire?
questions.fact: It was built on an island and fed by chinampas, artificial garden plots floating in the surrounding lake.

questions.prompt: Who was the first woman to be awarded a Nobel Prize?
questions.fact: She went on to win a second, in a different science, and remains the only person ever to manage that.

questions.prompt: Which empire was ruled by the Habsburg family for most of its existence?
questions.fact: The family expanded largely by marriage rather than conquest, which is why a line about others waging war became their motto.

questions.prompt: The Domesday Book was a survey of which country?
questions.fact: Compiled in 1086, it recorded holdings in such detail that its findings were treated as final, which is where the name comes from.

questions.prompt: Which country's flag was the first to be planted on the Moon?
questions.fact: It was stiffened with a horizontal rod, because there is no air on the Moon to make a flag hang open.

questions.prompt: Who was the first Prime Minister of independent India?
questions.fact: His speech that night, given as midnight struck, is remembered by the phrase about a tryst with destiny.

questions.prompt: Which Egyptian structure was the tallest building on Earth for around 3,800 years?
questions.fact: It only lost the record to Lincoln Cathedral in England, whose spire later collapsed and was never rebuilt.

questions.prompt: Which disaster struck the passenger liner Titanic in 1912?
questions.fact: The wreck was not located until 1985, and the search was partly cover for a classified mission to find two sunken submarines.

questions.prompt: Which two countries fought the Hundred Years' War?
questions.fact: It ran 116 years, and was not one continuous war but a series of conflicts with long truces between them.

questions.prompt: The Boston Tea Party was a protest against what?
questions.fact: The tea destroyed was worth roughly a million dollars in today's money, and the ships themselves were left untouched.

questions.prompt: Which ancient civilisation is credited with inventing concrete used in domes and aqueducts?
questions.fact: Their seawater harbour concrete grows stronger over time, a property modern cement does not share.

questions.prompt: Which conflict is often called the war to end all wars?
questions.fact: The phrase came from a book by H.G. Wells and was already being used sarcastically within a decade.

questions.prompt: Which document begins with the words We the People?
questions.fact: The original draft opened by listing the states individually. It was shortened when nobody could be sure which would ratify.

questions.prompt: Which sea did Moses part according to the biblical account of the Exodus?
questions.fact: The Hebrew phrase is closer to sea of reeds, which some scholars think points to marshland rather than open water.

questions.prompt: The Great Depression began with a stock market crash in which year?
questions.fact: The market did not return to its pre-crash level until 1954, a quarter of a century later.

questions.prompt: Which explorer is credited with first sighting the Pacific from the Americas?
questions.fact: He crossed Panama on foot in 1513, and was executed six years later by a rival who had him charged with treason.

questions.prompt: Which structure divided East and West Germany's most famous city?
questions.fact: Around 140 people died attempting to cross it, and roughly 5,000 succeeded, several by tunnelling underneath.

questions.prompt: Which Roman emperor is said to have made his horse a senator?
questions.fact: The story comes from hostile sources written decades later, and most historians now read it as a joke about the Senate.

questions.prompt: The Magna Carta was signed at which location?
questions.fact: The site was chosen as neutral ground in a meadow, because neither the barons nor the king trusted the other indoors.

questions.prompt: Which ancient people are credited with developing the first known alphabet?
questions.fact: Nearly every alphabet in use today, including Greek, Latin, Arabic and Hebrew, descends from theirs.

questions.prompt: Who was the first European known to reach India by sea around Africa?
questions.fact: The voyage took him longer to cross the Indian Ocean than the entire Atlantic leg, because he had to wait on the monsoon.

questions.prompt: Which US president resigned over the Watergate scandal?
questions.fact: He remains the only US president to resign the office, and was pardoned by his successor a month later.

questions.prompt: The Terracotta Army was built to guard the tomb of a ruler of which country?
questions.fact: The figures were originally painted in bright colours, most of which flaked away within minutes of being exposed to air.

questions.prompt: Which city hosted the conference that divided post-war Europe in February 1945?
questions.fact: It was held in a Crimean palace, chosen because the ailing US president could not manage a longer journey.

questions.prompt: Which medieval trade alliance dominated northern European commerce?
questions.fact: It had no army, no capital and no constitution, yet at its height it could blockade entire kingdoms into submission.

questions.prompt: Who was the last Tsar of Russia?
questions.fact: He kept a detailed diary throughout the revolution, and its entries are strikingly preoccupied with the weather.

questions.prompt: What is the chemical symbol for potassium?
questions.fact: It comes from kalium, the Latin name, which is itself borrowed from an Arabic word for plant ash.

questions.prompt: Which force causes objects to fall toward the Earth?
questions.fact: It is by far the weakest of the four fundamental forces. A fridge magnet outmuscles the entire planet.

questions.prompt: Which organ in the human body regenerates most readily after damage?
questions.fact: As little as a quarter of it can regrow to full size, which is what makes living donor transplants possible.

questions.prompt: What is the term for a substance that cannot be broken down chemically?
questions.fact: Ninety-four occur naturally on Earth. Everything past those has only ever existed inside a laboratory.

questions.prompt: Which type of animal is a Komodo dragon?
questions.fact: It is the largest lizard alive, and its bite delivers venom that stops a wound from clotting.

questions.prompt: What does a seismograph record?
questions.fact: The instrument works by keeping one mass still while everything around it shakes, then measuring the difference.

questions.prompt: Which planet has the most confirmed moons?
questions.fact: The count keeps changing as surveys find more small ones, and Saturn and Jupiter have swapped the lead repeatedly.

questions.prompt: Which part of the eye controls how much light enters?
questions.fact: Its pattern is essentially unique to each person and stable through life, which is why it works for identification.

questions.prompt: What is the process by which plants lose water through their leaves?
questions.fact: A large tree can move hundreds of litres a day this way, and the pull is what drags water up from the roots.

questions.prompt: Which scientist is credited with the discovery of the electron?
questions.fact: He proposed atoms were a soup of electrons in positive charge, a model his own student later demolished.

questions.prompt: Which blood component is responsible for clotting?
questions.fact: They are not whole cells but fragments shed from much larger cells in the bone marrow.

questions.prompt: What is the study of weather called?
questions.fact: Its name comes from the Greek for things high in the air, which originally included shooting stars.

questions.prompt: Which subatomic particle has no electric charge?
questions.fact: Outside an atomic nucleus one survives only about fifteen minutes before decaying into other particles.

questions.prompt: What is the largest structure in the human skeleton by volume?
questions.fact: It fuses from three separate bones during adolescence, which is why a child's is more flexible than an adult's.

questions.prompt: Which gas do fireflies use in the reaction that makes them glow?
questions.fact: The reaction is nearly 100 percent efficient, wasting almost no energy as heat, which no light bulb comes close to.

questions.prompt: Which layer of the Sun do we actually see from Earth?
questions.fact: Light made in the core takes tens of thousands of years to fight its way out to this layer, then eight minutes to reach us.

questions.prompt: What is the hardest known naturally occurring metal?
questions.fact: It is what makes stainless steel stainless, forming an invisible oxide layer that reseals itself when scratched.

questions.prompt: Which human sense is most closely linked to memory and emotion?
questions.fact: Its signals reach the emotional centres of the brain almost directly, bypassing the relay every other sense goes through.

questions.prompt: What is a light-year a measure of?
questions.fact: It is roughly 9.5 trillion kilometres, and the nearest star to the Sun sits about 4.2 of them away.

questions.prompt: Which chemical process turns grape juice into wine?
questions.fact: Yeast does the work, and it stops when the alcohol it produces reaches a level that kills it.

questions.prompt: How many pairs of chromosomes does a typical human cell contain?
questions.fact: Chimpanzees have 24 pairs. Two of theirs fused into one of ours, and the seam is still visible in the sequence.

questions.prompt: What is the term for a mixture of two or more metals?
questions.fact: Bronze was the first widely used one, and adding a little tin to copper made a metal hard enough to name an age after.

questions.prompt: Which body part contains the smallest bones in the human body?
questions.fact: The smallest is about the size of a grain of rice, and all three reach full adult size before birth.

questions.prompt: What kind of energy is stored in a stretched spring?
questions.fact: The same principle powers mechanical watches, where a coiled spring releases its store over roughly forty hours.

questions.prompt: Which organ produces the hormone adrenaline?
questions.fact: They sit on top of the kidneys, which is exactly what their name describes.

questions.prompt: What is the term for rock formed from cooled lava at the surface?
questions.fact: Cooling fast leaves no time for crystals to grow, which is why some of it comes out as natural glass.

questions.prompt: Which nutrient group provides the most energy per gram?
questions.fact: It carries more than twice the energy of the other two, which is why animals store reserves as fat rather than sugar.

questions.prompt: What is the name of the galaxy that contains our solar system?
questions.fact: It is on a collision course with Andromeda, though the two are so empty that almost no stars will actually hit.

questions.prompt: In which sport is the Stanley Cup awarded?
questions.fact: Every player on the winning team traditionally gets it for a day, and it has been used as a cereal bowl and a dog dish.

questions.prompt: How many points is a standard basket worth inside the three-point line?
questions.fact: The three-point line only arrived in the NBA in 1979, and was widely dismissed as a gimmick at the time.

questions.prompt: Which country hosts the Monaco Grand Prix?
questions.fact: The circuit runs on public roads, and the barriers and grandstands are assembled and removed every year.

questions.prompt: What is the maximum score from a single throw in darts?
questions.fact: Triple twenty is the highest single-dart score, which is why the twenty sits at the top of the board rather than the bullseye.

questions.prompt: Which sport features the positions setter and libero?
questions.fact: The libero wears a different coloured shirt and is barred from attacking, existing purely to improve defence.

questions.prompt: How long is a standard Olympic marathon swimming race?
questions.fact: It is held in open water, and races have been cancelled over water temperature rather than weather.

questions.prompt: Which country invented the sport of rugby?
questions.fact: The origin story of a schoolboy picking up the ball and running is almost certainly a later invention.

questions.prompt: In tennis, what is the term for winning a point directly from the serve?
questions.fact: The fastest recorded serves exceed 250 km/h, giving the receiver under half a second to react.

questions.prompt: Which sport uses a ball with 32 panels in its traditional design?
questions.fact: The pattern of twenty hexagons and twelve pentagons became standard at the 1970 World Cup, chosen to show up on black-and-white television.

questions.prompt: How many players are on a baseball team's fielding side?
questions.fact: The pitcher and catcher are together called the battery, a term borrowed from artillery.

questions.prompt: Which athletics event combines ten disciplines over two days?
questions.fact: Its winner has traditionally been called the world's greatest athlete, a phrase attributed to a king of Sweden.

questions.prompt: In which sport would you use a shuttlecock made from goose feathers?
questions.fact: Sixteen feathers are used, and they must all come from the same wing or the flight wobbles.

questions.prompt: Which competition is contested by the best golfers of Europe and the United States?
questions.fact: It was originally Britain against the United States. Continental Europe was added in 1979 to make it competitive.

questions.prompt: What is a perfect score in Olympic gymnastics under the old scoring system?
questions.fact: The scoreboard could not display it the first time it was achieved in 1976, so it showed 1.00 instead.

questions.prompt: Which sport is played on the largest standard field?
questions.fact: A full-size pitch is around nine football fields in area, which is part of why the sport stayed expensive.

questions.prompt: Which winter sport involves sliding head-first down an ice track?
questions.fact: Riders reach around 130 km/h with their chin a few centimetres above the ice, steering mostly by shifting their shoulders.

questions.prompt: In cricket, what is the term for three wickets in three consecutive balls?
questions.fact: The bowler traditionally received an actual hat from his club, which is where the phrase entered every other sport.

questions.prompt: What does a yellow card signify in football?
questions.fact: The idea came from traffic lights, after a referee struggled to make himself understood across a language barrier.

questions.prompt: Which sport is associated with Wimbledon's Centre Court?
questions.fact: The grass is cut to exactly eight millimetres, and the surface is rested for most of the year.

questions.prompt: How many holes must a golfer complete to make the cut in a standard major?
questions.fact: Roughly half the field goes home at that point, and missing it usually means earning nothing at all for the week.

questions.prompt: Which sport features terms like pin, escape and takedown?
questions.fact: It appeared in the ancient Olympics and is one of very few sports on the programme of the first modern Games too.

questions.prompt: In which sport do competitors ride a wave standing on a board?
questions.fact: Judges score the ride rather than the wave, and competitors are limited in how many waves they may take.

questions.prompt: Which trophy is awarded to the winner of the men's football World Cup?
questions.fact: The original trophy was won outright by Brazil in 1970, then stolen in 1983 and never recovered.

questions.prompt: How many rings must a gymnast use in the men's rings apparatus?
questions.fact: The rings must not visibly swing during a hold, so the difficulty is as much about stillness as strength.

questions.prompt: Which sport uses the terms bogey, par and eagle?
questions.fact: Bogey originally meant the score a good player should make, before par took over that role and bogey slipped a shot.

questions.prompt: In which sport is the Tour de France's polka-dot jersey awarded?
questions.fact: The design was chosen by a sponsor whose sweet wrappers used the same pattern.

questions.prompt: How many players from each side contest a game of beach volleyball?
questions.fact: There is no rotation and no positions, so both players must be able to do everything.

questions.prompt: Which sport features a piste, a foil and a riposte?
questions.fact: It is one of only five sports to have featured at every modern Olympic Games.

questions.prompt: Which film features a hotel called the Overlook?
questions.fact: Its author disliked the adaptation enough to fund a second, more faithful version for television twenty years later.

questions.prompt: Which streaming series features the Hawkins National Laboratory?
questions.fact: Its title font is a 1980s book-jacket typeface, chosen so the show looked like a paperback before a frame was shot.

questions.prompt: Which actor voiced Darth Vader in the original Star Wars trilogy?
questions.fact: The actor inside the suit spoke every line on set, and only discovered at the premiere that his voice had been replaced.

questions.prompt: Which video game franchise features a character called Lara Croft?
questions.fact: Her distinctive angular look was partly an accident of early hardware, which could not render smooth curves cheaply.

questions.prompt: Which sitcom features the characters Michael Scott and Dwight Schrute?
questions.fact: It adapted a British series whose creators expected it to fail, since the original ran only twelve episodes by design.

questions.prompt: Which singer is known as the King of Pop?
questions.fact: The moonwalk he made famous had been performed by street dancers for years before he put it on television.

questions.prompt: Which film franchise features a character named Dominic Toretto?
questions.fact: It began as a small film about street racing, based on a magazine article about illegal races in New York.

questions.prompt: Which Japanese art form of comics is read right to left?
questions.fact: English editions once flipped the artwork to read left to right, until publishers found readers preferred the original layout.

questions.prompt: Which film is set aboard the Nostromo?
questions.fact: The cast were not shown the creature before the chest scene, so their reactions are close to genuine.

questions.prompt: Which streaming platform produced the series Squid Game?
questions.fact: Its writer spent a decade failing to sell the script, at one point selling his laptop to cover living costs.

questions.prompt: Which fashion week is not one of the traditional big four?
questions.fact: Paris completes the four, and the order they run in has barely changed in decades.

questions.prompt: Which animated series features the town of South Park?
questions.fact: Episodes are famously made in about a week, which lets them respond to news that broke days earlier.

questions.prompt: Which actor played the Joker in the 2008 film The Dark Knight?
questions.fact: He kept a diary in character during filming, and won a posthumous Academy Award for the performance.

questions.prompt: Which instrument is Jimi Hendrix most associated with?
questions.fact: He played right-handed instruments upside down, restringing them, which changed the tone in ways guitarists still chase.

questions.prompt: Which TV series is set in the fictional Yorkshire village of Emmerdale?
questions.fact: It began as a daytime programme called Emmerdale Farm and only dropped the farm from its title in 1989.

questions.prompt: Which film won the Academy Award for Best Picture in 1994?
questions.fact: Its two main rivals that year are now more highly rated by audiences than the winner.

questions.prompt: Which pop group performed Wannabe?
questions.fact: The video was shot in a single take on a shoestring budget, in a hotel due for demolition.

questions.prompt: Which director is known for the films Vertigo and Rear Window?
questions.fact: He appeared briefly in most of his own films, and moved the cameos early so audiences would stop hunting for him mid-plot.

questions.prompt: Which card game inspired a hugely popular series of televised tournaments?
questions.fact: Televised play only took off once tables were fitted with small cameras that let viewers see the hidden cards.

questions.prompt: Which film features the line about there being no place like home?
questions.fact: The ruby slippers were silver in the original book. They were changed to show off colour film.

questions.prompt: Which television talent show format originated in the United Kingdom in 2001?
questions.fact: It became American Idol a year later, and the format has since been licensed to over forty countries.

questions.prompt: Which band is fronted by Chris Martin?
questions.fact: They formed at university in London and used four different band names before settling on the current one.

questions.prompt: Which superhero team includes Cyclops, Storm and Wolverine?
questions.fact: The 1975 relaunch that made them famous deliberately assembled an international line-up to sell the comic overseas.

questions.prompt: Which film is set largely on the planet Arrakis?
questions.fact: An earlier attempt to film it in the 1970s collapsed, but its concept art shaped science fiction design for decades.

questions.prompt: Which social media platform was originally limited to 140 characters per post?
questions.fact: The limit came from text messages, which allowed 160 characters, leaving twenty for the username.

questions.prompt: Which actress played Hermione Granger in the Harry Potter films?
questions.fact: She was nine at her first audition and had never acted professionally before being cast.

questions.prompt: Which country's cinema is known as Nollywood?
questions.fact: It produces more films per year than Hollywood, most shot in a matter of weeks and released straight to video.

questions.prompt: Which soft drink brand's logo uses a distinctive red and white script?
questions.fact: The script was written by the company bookkeeper in 1886 and has barely changed since.

questions.prompt: Which country has the most natural lakes?
questions.fact: It holds more lake area than the rest of the world combined, nearly all of it carved by retreating ice sheets.

questions.prompt: Which sea lies between Turkey and Ukraine?
questions.fact: Below about 150 metres it has almost no oxygen, which has preserved ancient shipwrecks in remarkable condition.

questions.prompt: Which African country was never colonised by a European power?
questions.fact: It defeated an invading Italian army at Adwa in 1896, one of the few decisive African victories of that era.

questions.prompt: Which strait connects the Mediterranean to the Black Sea?
questions.fact: Istanbul sits on both banks, making it the only major city in the world spanning two continents.

questions.prompt: What is the capital of Australia?
questions.fact: It was built from nothing as a compromise, because Sydney and Melbourne could not agree which should take the role.

questions.prompt: Which is the second-largest country by land area?
questions.fact: Roughly nine in ten of its people live within about 160 kilometres of the southern border.

questions.prompt: Which two seas does the Panama Canal connect?
questions.fact: Because of the isthmus's shape, a ship heading for the Pacific actually travels south-east through it.

questions.prompt: Which country contains the world's largest coffee-growing region?
questions.fact: It has led world production for over 150 years, and a single bad frost there can move global prices.

questions.prompt: Which is the deepest lake in Africa?
questions.fact: It reaches over 1,400 metres and holds around 16 percent of the world's available fresh water.

questions.prompt: Which European country has the most active volcano in the region?
questions.fact: Mount Etna has erupted almost continuously for thousands of years, and towns on its slopes simply rebuild around the lava.

questions.prompt: Which country's territory includes the southernmost city in the world?
questions.fact: Puerto Williams holds the title, though nearby Ushuaia in Argentina is far better known for claiming it.

questions.prompt: What is the official language of Brazil?
questions.fact: It is the only Portuguese-speaking country in the Americas, a result of a 1494 treaty drawing a line down the Atlantic.

questions.prompt: Which island is divided between Haiti and the Dominican Republic?
questions.fact: The border is visible from orbit, with dense forest on one side and cleared land on the other.

questions.prompt: Which is the largest sea entirely within one country's borders?
questions.fact: It sits wholly within Turkey and links the Black Sea to the Aegean through two narrow straits.

questions.prompt: Which continent has the most countries?
questions.fact: It has 54, a number that owes more to the borders drawn in Berlin in 1885 than to anything on the ground.

questions.prompt: Which sea is the world's largest inland body of water?
questions.fact: Whether it counts as a sea or a lake is a live legal question, because the answer changes how its oil is divided.

questions.prompt: Which city is served by Schiphol Airport?
questions.fact: The airport sits about four metres below sea level, on the bed of a lake drained in the 1850s.

questions.prompt: Which is the world's longest mountain range, including underwater sections?
questions.fact: It runs some 16,000 kilometres along the ocean floor, and Iceland is one of the few places it breaks the surface.

questions.prompt: Which country has the largest Muslim population?
questions.fact: It is spread across more than 17,000 islands, which is part of why its national motto is about unity in diversity.

questions.prompt: Which US state has the longest coastline?
questions.fact: Its coastline is longer than all the other states put together, thanks to an enormously indented shore.

questions.prompt: Which capital city sits on the Tiber river?
questions.fact: The river's flooding was so destructive that high walls were built along it in the 1870s, cutting the city off from its own water.

questions.prompt: Which country is entirely surrounded by Italy apart from one neighbour?
questions.fact: It claims to be the world's oldest surviving republic, dating its founding to the year 301.

questions.prompt: Which ocean lies between Africa and Australia?
questions.fact: It is the warmest ocean, which limits how much oxygen its water can hold and shapes what lives in it.

questions.prompt: Which city is the largest in Canada by population?
questions.fact: More than half its residents were born outside Canada, one of the highest proportions of any large city on Earth.

questions.prompt: Which sea separates Sweden from Latvia?
questions.fact: Its water is barely salty, because so many rivers drain into a sea with only one narrow outlet.

questions.prompt: Which country has the highest population density among large nations?
questions.fact: It packs roughly the population of Russia into an area smaller than the US state of Iowa.

questions.prompt: Which river forms much of the border between Brazil and Argentina?
questions.fact: It is South America's second-longest river, and its dams supply a large share of both countries' electricity.

questions.prompt: Which country was formerly known as Burma?
questions.fact: Both names come from the same root, and which one a government uses has long carried political weight.

questions.prompt: Which novel features a boy stranded at sea with a tiger?
options: The Old Man and the Sea
questions.fact: It was rejected by several London publishers before winning the Booker Prize.

questions.prompt: Which poet is associated with the phrase I wandered lonely as a cloud?
questions.fact: His sister's journal describes the same daffodils two years earlier, in prose many readers find better than the poem.

questions.prompt: Which novel is set in the fictional town of Maycomb?
questions.fact: Its author published nothing else for fifty-five years, and the eventual second book was an early draft of the first.

questions.prompt: Which author created the detective Philip Marlowe?
questions.fact: He only started writing fiction at forty-four, after losing an oil executive job during the Depression.

questions.prompt: Which novel opens on a farm called Green Gables?
questions.fact: It became so popular in Japan that the setting is a pilgrimage site for Japanese visitors to Prince Edward Island.

questions.prompt: Who wrote the play A Streetcar Named Desire?
questions.fact: The streetcar line in its title was real, running through New Orleans to a street actually named Desire.

questions.prompt: Which epic poem tells of the founding of Rome?
questions.fact: Its author asked for it to be burned unfinished. The emperor overruled him after his death.

questions.prompt: Which novel features the character Winston Smith?
questions.fact: The title is often said to be a reversal of 1948, the year it was written, though its author never confirmed it.

questions.prompt: Which novel begins in a place called the Shire?
questions.fact: Its author drew the maps first and insisted the geography had to work before the plot could move through it.

questions.prompt: Which novel features a whale called the White Whale?
questions.fact: It was inspired partly by a real whale that reportedly attacked ships off Chile and survived dozens of harpoons.

questions.prompt: Which novel is narrated by a character called Scout?
questions.fact: The narrator is an adult looking back, which is why the voice shifts between a child's view and a grown-up's.

questions.prompt: Which term describes a comparison using like or as?
questions.fact: The difference from a metaphor is only the signal word, which is why the two get confused so often.

questions.prompt: Who wrote The Hitchhiker's Guide to the Galaxy?
questions.fact: It started as a radio series, and he was famously so late with deadlines that publishers locked him in a hotel to finish one book.

questions.prompt: Which Russian author wrote the short story The Overcoat?
questions.fact: A famous remark holds that all Russian literature came out from under this one coat.

questions.prompt: Which novel features the character Sydney Carton?
questions.fact: Its closing line about a far, far better thing is among the most quoted endings in English fiction.

questions.prompt: Who wrote the novel Things Fall Apart's most famous African successor, Half of a Yellow Sun?
questions.fact: It is set during the Biafran war, which her own parents lived through and rarely spoke about.

questions.prompt: Which form of poem traditionally has five lines and a humorous tone?
questions.fact: The name comes from an Irish city, though nobody has satisfactorily explained the connection.

questions.prompt: Which novel is set at Manderley?
questions.fact: Its opening line about dreaming of Manderley is regularly voted among the best in English fiction.

questions.prompt: Which poet wrote the collection Ariel?
questions.fact: The collection was assembled and published after her death, in an order she had not chosen.

questions.prompt: Which author wrote the Earthsea series?
questions.fact: She wrote its protagonist as dark-skinned in 1968, and spent decades objecting to cover artists who ignored it.

questions.prompt: Which term describes the turning point of a narrative?
questions.fact: In classical structure it sits at the centre, not the end, with everything after it working out the consequences.

questions.prompt: Which play features the characters Rosencrantz and Guildenstern as leads?
questions.fact: It takes two minor characters from Hamlet and follows them offstage, where they have no idea what is happening.

questions.prompt: Which novel opens with a family fleeing the Oklahoma Dust Bowl?
questions.fact: Its author spent months living in migrant camps before writing a word of it.

questions.prompt: Which literary award is presented annually for fiction written in English and published in the UK?
questions.fact: It has been shared between two winners three times, after which the rules were changed to forbid it.

questions.prompt: Who wrote the novel Great Expectations?
questions.fact: Nearly all his novels were serialised, which is why they are so long and end so many chapters on a hook.

questions.prompt: Which poem features the line water, water, every where?
options: The Rime of the Ancient Mariner
questions.fact: The albatross hung around the sailor's neck gave English a phrase for a burden you cannot put down.

questions.prompt: Which author wrote the novel Beloved's Pulitzer-winning contemporary, The Color Purple?
questions.fact: She coined the term womanist, arguing feminism as then framed did not describe her experience.

questions.prompt: Which term describes a word that imitates a sound?
questions.fact: Different languages disagree about the sounds animals make, which suggests the imitation is less direct than it feels.

questions.prompt: What does the acronym RAM's opposite storage type ROM stand for?
questions.fact: Its contents are written once at manufacture, which is why the earliest game cartridges could not be saved to.

questions.prompt: Which company created the first commercially successful spreadsheet program?
questions.fact: VisiCalc sold so many Apple IIs that it became the first program credited with selling the computer it ran on.

questions.prompt: What is the name for software distributed with its source code freely available?
questions.fact: Free in this sense refers to liberty rather than price, a distinction its advocates have spent decades explaining.

questions.prompt: What does the acronym IP stand for in IP address?
questions.fact: The original scheme allowed about 4.3 billion addresses, a number thought absurdly generous when it was chosen.

questions.prompt: Which programming language is named after a British comedy troupe?
questions.fact: Its official tutorials once used spam and eggs as example values, following the same joke.

questions.prompt: What is the purpose of a compiler?
options: To run code line by line
To translate source code into machine code
questions.fact: The first one was written by Grace Hopper, who had to argue that a computer could usefully write its own programs.

questions.prompt: Which company developed the first widely used graphical user interface?
questions.fact: Its research centre invented the mouse-driven desktop, the laser printer and Ethernet, and commercialised almost none of it.

questions.prompt: What does a modem do?
questions.fact: The name is a contraction of modulator-demodulator, describing the two halves of the job.

questions.prompt: Which file format is designed for lossless image compression?
questions.fact: It was created specifically to replace GIF after the company holding GIF's compression patent began demanding fees.

questions.prompt: What is the term for a duplicate copy of data kept for safety?
questions.fact: The standard advice is three copies on two kinds of media with one kept off site, usually shortened to three-two-one.

questions.prompt: Which company produced the Walkman?
questions.fact: It had no recording function, which the company's own engineers thought would doom it.

questions.prompt: What does the acronym AI stand for?
questions.fact: The term was coined for a 1956 workshop whose organisers expected significant progress over a single summer.

questions.prompt: Which technology allows contactless card payments?
questions.fact: Its range is a few centimetres by design, since being hard to intercept is the point rather than a limitation.

questions.prompt: What is a pixel?
options: The smallest element of a digital image
questions.fact: The word is a contraction of picture element, and modern phone screens pack them tighter than the eye can resolve.

questions.prompt: What does the acronym GIF stand for?
questions.fact: Its creator insisted the name is pronounced with a soft g, and lost that argument comprehensively.

questions.prompt: Which part of a computer permanently stores the operating system?
questions.fact: Solid state drives replaced spinning disks largely because they have no moving parts to fail or wait for.

questions.prompt: What is the term for testing a website with two versions to compare results?
questions.fact: Large sites run hundreds simultaneously, which means almost no two visitors see quite the same page.

questions.prompt: What does a router do on a network?
questions.fact: Every packet you send crosses a dozen or more of them, each deciding independently where to pass it next.

questions.prompt: What is the main function of a GPU?
questions.fact: Its knack for doing thousands of simple sums at once is why it ended up powering machine learning.

questions.prompt: Which early computer network was funded by the US Department of Defense?
questions.fact: The idea that it was built to survive a nuclear war is disputed; its designers say it was mostly about sharing scarce computers.

questions.prompt: What does the acronym QR stand for in QR code?
questions.fact: It was invented to track car parts, and its creator chose not to enforce the patent, which is why it spread everywhere.

questions.prompt: Which company makes the Xbox games console?
questions.fact: It grew out of a proposal to stop Sony's console becoming the main computer in the living room.

questions.prompt: What is a cookie in a web browser?
options: A small data file stored by a site
questions.fact: The name comes from magic cookie, an older programming term for a token passed back and forth unchanged.

questions.prompt: Which measure describes how much data a connection can carry?
questions.fact: It is often confused with speed, but a high-bandwidth link with high latency still feels slow to use.

questions.prompt: Which programming paradigm organises code around objects and classes?
questions.fact: Its originator later said he had meant to emphasise messages between objects rather than the objects themselves.

questions.prompt: What does the acronym USB-C describe?
questions.fact: European law now requires it on most new phones, which finally settled a decades-long argument about chargers.

questions.prompt: Which company developed the PageRank algorithm?
questions.fact: It ranked pages by who linked to them, treating a link as a vote, which is why link-selling became an industry.

questions.prompt: What is the purpose of two-factor authentication?
questions.fact: Codes sent by text are the weakest common form, because a phone number can be transferred away from its owner.
